principles.content: Cancer represents evolution occurring among somatic cells.
Three conditions must exist for evolution to occur: Variation, Heritability, and Selection.
Cells acquire genetic and epigenetic changes that create diversity.
depends_on: Cancer represents evolution occurring among somatic cells.

principles.content: These changes are passed to daughter cells during division.
depends_on: Cells acquire genetic and epigenetic changes that create diversity.

principles.content: Cells with advantageous characteristics survive and expand.
depends_on: Three conditions must exist for evolution to occur: Variation, Heritability, and Selection.

principles.content: Cancer does not create new biological mechanisms. Instead, it exploits pathways that normally regulate growth, repair, development, and survival.
Cancer cells can activate EGFR signaling continuously to drive proliferation.
depends_on: Cancer does not create new biological mechanisms. Instead, it exploits pathways that normally regulate growth, repair, development, and survival.

principles.content: VEGF promotes blood vessel formation during wound healing, but tumors exploit it for their own supply.
Telomerase maintains stem cell populations, but cancer cells reactivate it for unlimited replication.
PD-L1 helps prevent excessive immune activation, but tumors use it to suppress immune destruction.
Cancer represents normal biology operating without regulation.
Cancer develops when DNA information becomes corrupted through mutations, amplifications, deletions, rearrangements, methylation, or chromatin regulation.
Corrupted DNA information alters cell division, cell death, signal response, and environment interaction.
depends_on: Cancer develops when DNA information becomes corrupted through mutations, amplifications, deletions, rearrangements, methylation, or chromatin regulation.

principles.content: Cancer behavior reflects accumulated changes in its biological information system.
depends_on: Cancer develops when DNA information becomes corrupted through mutations, amplifications, deletions, rearrangements, methylation, or chromatin regulation.

principles.content: Cancer characteristics are interconnected.
Cancer characteristics include uncontrolled proliferation, resistance to cell death, genomic instability, immune escape, angiogenesis, and invasion.
depends_on: Cancer characteristics are interconnected.

principles.content: Metastasis and cellular regulation are interconnected.
A single mutation can influence multiple cancer behaviors.
TP53 loss impairs DNA repair.
depends_on: A single mutation can influence multiple cancer behaviors.

principles.content: TP53 loss reduces apoptosis.
depends_on: A single mutation can influence multiple cancer behaviors.

principles.content: TP53 loss causes genomic instability.
depends_on: A single mutation can influence multiple cancer behaviors.

principles.content: TP53 loss increases mutation accumulation.

principles.content: TP53 loss enhances tumor evolution.

principles.content: KRAS activation alters metabolism.

principles.content: Cancer biology is a network of interacting processes.
The tumor microenvironment is part of the cancer.
A tumor includes fibroblasts, immune cells, endothelial cells, extracellular matrix, signaling molecules, and metabolic factors.
depends_on: The tumor microenvironment is part of the cancer.

principles.content: Tumors actively reshape their environment to support growth, invasion, angiogenesis, immune suppression, and resistance to treatment.
depends_on: The tumor microenvironment is part of the cancer.

principles.content: Tumor behavior is determined by both malignant cells and their surrounding ecosystem.
Cancer exists under constant selective pressure.
Tumors are eliminated by pressures including oxygen limitation, nutrient scarcity, immune surveillance, chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted therapy.
depends_on: Cancer exists under constant selective pressure

principles.content: Sensitive cancer cells are eliminated, while resistant cells survive and expand.
depends_on: Tumors are eliminated by pressures including oxygen limitation, nutrient scarcity, immune surveillance, chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted therapy

principles.content: Cancers relapse after initially successful treatment, metastatic disease differs from the original tumor, and resistance develops over time.
depends_on: Tumors are eliminated by pressures including oxygen limitation, nutrient scarcity, immune surveillance, chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted therapy

principles.content: Every therapy creates a new environment in which cancer cells must adapt.
depends_on: Cancer exists under constant selective pressure

principles.content: Cancer cells must generate sufficient energy and cellular building blocks to support continuous growth.
Tumors alter glucose metabolism, amino acid metabolism, lipid synthesis, mitochondrial function, and nutrient sensing pathways to support continuous growth.
depends_on: Cancer cells must generate sufficient energy and cellular building blocks to support continuous growth

principles.content: The Warburg effect is an example of metabolic adaptation where cancer cells preferentially use glycolysis despite available oxygen.
depends_on: Tumors alter glucose metabolism, amino acid metabolism, lipid synthesis, mitochondrial function, and nutrient sensing pathways to support continuous growth

principles.content: Cancer progression follows a recurring pattern of initiation, clonal expansion, diversification, selection, microenvironment remodeling, dissemination, therapeutic selection, and relapse
Initiation occurs when a normal cell acquires an alteration providing a survival advantage
depends_on: Cancer progression follows a recurring pattern of initiation, clonal expansion, diversification, selection, microenvironment remodeling, dissemination, therapeutic selection, and relapse

Uncontrolled growth is a strategy for evolving cell populations to survive and expand.

principles.content: The immune system detects and eliminates nascent transformed cells.
Cells have internal anti-cancer programs to stop the cell cycle, trigger repair, or induce apoptosis when DNA damage is excessive.
Small populations of tumor cells can persist but are held in check by the immune system.
Subclones of tumor cells can evolve to evade control and lead to clinically apparent cancer.
Cells can accumulate DNA damage from replication errors, inflammation, radiation, and toxins.
Most damaged cells are repaired, forced into senescence, or eliminated by apoptosis.
The immune system helps recognize and clear damaged cells that slip through intrinsic checkpoints.
depends_on: Cells have internal anti-cancer programs to stop the cell cycle, trigger repair, or induce apoptosis when DNA damage is excessive.

principles.content: The immune system can hold small populations of tumor cells in check.
depends_on: Small populations of tumor cells can persist but are held in check by the immune system.

principles.content: Subclones of tumor cells can evade control by evolving to evade the immune system.
depends_on: Subclones of tumor cells can evolve to evade control and lead to clinically apparent cancer.

principles.content: In hypoxic conditions, cells may accumulate more DNA damage.
depends_on: Cells can accumulate DNA damage from replication errors, inflammation, radiation, and toxins.

principles.content: Intrinsic cellular safeguards can push cells into senescence.
depends_on: Cells have internal anti-cancer programs to stop the cell cycle, trigger repair, or induce apoptosis when DNA damage is excessive.

principles.content: Senescent and apoptotic cells expose ‘eat me’ signals that attract phagocytes.
Phagocytes engulf debris and present abnormal peptides to T cells.
depends_on: Senescent and apoptotic cells expose ‘eat me’ signals that attract phagocytes.

principles.content: Cells under oncogenic or genotoxic stress upregulate surface molecules that flag them as ‘altered self’.
Precancerous cells increase ligands for activating receptors on NK cells.
depends_on: Cells under oncogenic or genotoxic stress upregulate surface molecules that flag them as ‘altered self’.

principles.content: NK cells recognize the imbalance between ‘normal self’ signals and ‘stress’ signals.
depends_on: Precancerous cells increase ligands for activating receptors on NK cells.

principles.content: NK cells release perforin and granzymes to induce apoptosis in stressed cells.
depends_on: NK cells recognize the imbalance between ‘normal self’ signals and ‘stress’ signals.

principles.content: Pattern-recognition receptors on macrophages and dendritic cells detect danger signals.
Innate immune cells constantly sample the environment for danger signals.
depends_on: Pattern-recognition receptors on macrophages and dendritic cells detect danger signals.

principles.content: Every cell has an internal alarm system (p53) that stops badly damaged cells from dividing.
NK cells act like bouncers, checking for a mismatched ID badge and killing on the spot.
depends_on: Every cell has an internal alarm system (p53) that stops badly damaged cells from dividing.

principles.content: Tumor cells express neoantigens: novel peptides derived from mutated proteins presented on MHC I molecules.
Tumor cells may overexpress normal self proteins at abnormal levels or in unusual contexts, creating tumor-associated antigens.
Dendritic cells ingest dying tumor or precancerous cells, process the proteins, and present peptide fragments on MHC molecules.
depends_on: Tumor cells express neoantigens: novel peptides derived from mutated proteins presented on MHC I molecules.

principles.content: Dendritic cells migrate to lymph nodes and prime naïve CD8 and CD4 T cells against these antigens.
depends_on: Dendritic cells ingest dying tumor or precancerous cells, process the proteins, and present peptide fragments on MHC molecules.

principles.content: Activated CD8 T cells patrol tissues and scan MHC I on cells for the specific tumor peptide they recognize.
depends_on: Dendritic cells migrate to lymph nodes and prime naïve CD8 and CD4 T cells against these antigens.

principles.content: Activated CD8 T cells form an immune synapse and release perforin and granzymes, triggering apoptosis of that single target cell.
depends_on: Activated CD8 T cells patrol tissues and scan MHC I on cells for the specific tumor peptide they recognize.

principles.content: Activated CD8 T cells can also engage death receptors (e.g., Fas–FasL) to induce programmed cell death.
depends_on: Activated CD8 T cells form an immune synapse and release perforin and granzymes, triggering apoptosis of that single target cell.

principles.content: Helper T cells provide cytokines (e.g., interferon-gamma) that increase MHC expression on tumor and stromal cells.
depends_on: Activated CD8 T cells can also engage death receptors (e.g., Fas–FasL) to induce programmed cell death.

principles.content: Helper T cells enhance the activity of macrophages and promote B-cell antibody production against tumor-associated antigens.
depends_on: Helper T cells provide cytokines (e.g., interferon-gamma) that increase MHC expression on tumor and stromal cells.

principles.content: Antibodies can bind surface antigens on tumor cells, flagging them for antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) by NK cells and other effector cells.
depends_on: Helper T cells enhance the activity of macrophages and promote B-cell antibody production against tumor-associated antigens.

principles.content: Complement activation on antibody-coated tumor cells can contribute to lysis or opsonization for phagocytosis.
depends_on: Antibodies can bind surface antigens on tumor cells, flagging them for antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) by NK cells and other effector cells.

principles.content: The immune system may contain small clusters of tumor cells so they divide and die at roughly the same rate, never forming a detectable mass.
CD8 and CD4 T cells, NK cells, and macrophages keep attacking, producing interferon-gamma and cytotoxic mediators that restrain growth.
depends_on: The immune system may contain small clusters of tumor cells so they divide and die at roughly the same rate, never forming a detectable mass.

principles.content: Tumor cells under this pressure may down-modulate immunogenic antigens or MHC I, or alter signaling pathways to resist apoptosis.
depends_on: CD8 and CD4 T cells, NK cells, and macrophages keep attacking, producing interferon-gamma and cytotoxic mediators that restrain growth.

principles.content: Downregulating MHC I so CTLs can no longer recognize tumor antigens effectively.
depends_on: The immune system may contain small clusters of tumor cells so they divide and die at roughly the same rate, never forming a detectable mass.

principles.content: Losing or editing the most immunogenic neoantigens, leaving only low-visibility subclones.
depends_on: The immune system may contain small clusters of tumor cells so they divide and die at roughly the same rate, never forming a detectable mass.

principles.content: Upregulating non-classical MHC molecules that inhibit NK cells despite reduced classical MHC I.
depends_on: The immune system may contain small clusters of tumor cells so they divide and die at roughly the same rate, never forming a detectable mass.

principles.content: T cells naturally have inhibitory checkpoints to prevent autoimmunity; tumors hijack these.
Tumor and stromal cells often overexpress ligands such as PD-L1 that bind PD-1 on T cells, sending a “stand down” signal.
depends_on: T cells naturally have inhibitory checkpoints to prevent autoimmunity; tumors hijack these.

principles.content: Many tumors upregulate other checkpoints like CTLA-4 signaling pathways that dampen T-cell activation.
depends_on: T cells naturally have inhibitory checkpoints to prevent autoimmunity; tumors hijack these.

principles.content: T cells remain present but less functional, with reduced cytokine production, proliferation, and cytotoxicity over time.
depends_on: T cells naturally have inhibitory checkpoints to prevent autoimmunity; tumors hijack these.

principles.content: Tumors secrete immunosuppressive cytokines like TGF-beta and IL-10 that blunt effector T cells and NK cells while promoting regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs).
Tumor-associated macrophages often shift toward a pro-tumor phenotype that supports angiogenesis, matrix remodeling, and suppression of local immune responses.
Abnormal vasculature and high interstitial pressure make it physically harder for effector T cells to infiltrate the tumor core.

If proliferation is very rapid, immune cells may simply not kill fast enough to prevent net growth, especially in the setting of systemic immune compromise (e.g., age, immunosuppressive drugs, chronic infection).

Cancer cells evolve like a fugitive learning to avoid cameras. They hide their ID (lower visibility), disable the “kill switch” T cells normally respect (checkpoints), and poison the neighborhood with signals that calm down nearby immune cells.
The immune system acts at multiple levels: preventive surveillance, targeted killing of cancer cells, and long-term control.
Preventive surveillance: clearing stressed, senescent, and precancerous cells via intrinsic checkpoints, NK cells, and phagocytes.
Targeted killing of cancer cells: CTLs, NK cells, antibodies, and helper T cells coordinate to recognize neoantigens and destroy malignant cells.
Long-term control: maintaining some tumors in a low-level equilibrium until they either get eliminated or evolve escape mechanisms.
Checkpoint inhibitors block inhibitory pathways like PD-1/PD-L1 or CTLA-4, “releasing the brakes” on T cells so they can resume attacking tumor cells.
CAR T cells and other engineered cell therapies enhance T-cell recognition of tumor antigens.
Cancer vaccines and oncolytic viruses aim to increase the visibility and immunogenicity of tumor cells and improve priming of adaptive responses.
The immune system can recognize and target cancer cells.
T cells can recognize cancer cells through the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules.
depends_on: The immune system can recognize and target cancer cells.

principles.content: Cancer cells can evade the immune system by suppressing the activity of T cells.
depends_on: T cells can recognize cancer cells through the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules.

principles.content: The immune system can be activated to target cancer cells through various mechanisms, including the use of checkpoint inhibitors.
Checkpoint inhibitors can release the brakes on T cells, allowing them to attack cancer cells more effectively.
depends_on: The immune system can be activated to target cancer cells through various mechanisms, including the use of checkpoint inhibitors.

principles.content: The immune system can also target cancer cells through the activation of natural killer cells.
Cancer cells can also be targeted through the use of immunotherapies that stimulate the immune system to attack cancer cells.
The immune system can be suppressed by cancer cells through various mechanisms, including the production of immunosuppressive molecules.
depends_on: The immune system can recognize and target cancer cells.

principles.content: Cancer cells can also evade the immune system by altering their surface proteins to avoid recognition by T cells.
depends_on: T cells can recognize cancer cells through the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules.
